proof:
# Genuine criticality restores the nearest-neighbor residual comparison
It does not prove a choice of original KKT rows satisfying OC, and does not
assert that the own-fiber hypothesis holds for every critical cap.

## 1. Statement

Let d>=2, let C be a full-dimensional compact convex body in R times R^d,
and use the mixed measure mu=sum_(j in Z) vol_d(C_j). Assume mu(C)>0.
All sums below are finite. Fibers of zero d-volume are retained as sets
where needed; their contribution to mu is zero. Set

    gamma=(d/(d+1))^d.

Suppose y=(i,x) belongs to C intersect (Z times R^d), the fiber C_i has
positive volume, and y is a GLOBAL maximizer of raw halfspace depth Q.
Let H be an actual closed ambient halfspace containing y with

    mu(C intersect H)=Q,
    p=|C_i intersect H_i|/|C_i|<=1/2.                     (1)

For every integer j put

    v_j=|C_j|^(1/d),
    f_j=|C_j minus H_j|^(1/d),

with zero values on absent or zero-volume fibers. Then the ORIGINAL
nearest-neighbor residual roots satisfy

    f_i >= (f_(i-1)+f_(i+1))/2.                         (2)

No three-fiber or global noheavy hypothesis is required. If at least
one neighboring STRICT residual set C_(i+/-1) minus H_(i+/-1) is empty,
then the inequality is strict. In that empty-neighbor case, if also
p<=gamma, it has the quantitative reserve

    f_i-(f_(i-1)+f_(i+1))/2
       > (sqrt(5)/3-5/7) v_i >0.                        (3)

The only global input is genuine criticality at a global deepest point,
which supplies both an available tilt comparison and Q>=gamma |C_j|
for every positive-volume fiber. Neither is automatic for a cap whose
mass is merely bounded by some unrelated number.

## 2. Elementary constants

For every integer d>=2,

    1/3<gamma<=4/9.                                    (4)

For the upper bound expand (1+1/d)^d: its first three terms are
1+1+(d-1)/(2d)>=9/4. For the lower bound, the binomial expansion is
bounded above by sum_(k>=0)1/k!<3. The latter strict inequality follows
from k!>=2^(k-1) for k>=2, with strict inequality for k>=3, and summing
the resulting geometric series. Therefore

    (1-gamma)^(1/d)>=(5/9)^(1/d)>=sqrt(5)/3>5/7.         (5)

The last comparison is equivalent to245>225.

## 3. If one neighboring residual is empty, the critical cap has a step

Translate the integer coordinate so i=0. Suppose first that the strict
residual at -1 is empty. The source residual is nonempty and has positive
volume because p<1. The set C minus H is convex: it is the intersection
of C with the strict complementary halfspace. Its projection on the
integer-coordinate axis is therefore an interval, possibly open at an
endpoint. If any fiber j<=-1 contained a strict residual point, joining
it to a strict residual point at base0 would produce one at -1 (for
j=-1 this is immediate). Consequently

    C_j subset H_j for EVERY integer j<0.               (6)

This is a set statement, not the inference that zero volume means an
empty set.

Write H={u.x+a z>=b}. Its continuous coefficient u is nonzero: otherwise
H contains the entire source fiber and p=1, contrary to(1). For L>=0
consider the single ambient halfspace

    H(L)={u.x+(a-L)z>=b}.

Its source trace is unchanged. On every j<0 the trace grows, but the
whole fiber is already captured by(6). On every j>0 the trace decreases.
For a sufficiently large finite L it strictly misses every positive-base
fiber, since there are finitely many compact nonempty integer fibers.
All H(L) continue to contain the same globally deepest point y. Their
masses must therefore be at least Q; their masses are also at most the
critical mass Q at L=0. Thus no mass can be lost. In particular the
ORIGINAL H has zero captured d-volume at every positive base, and

    Q=sum_(j<0) |C_j| + p |C_0|.                        (7)

If a neighboring strict residual on the right is empty instead, the
same proof with z replaced by -z gives the symmetric statement.
The argument includes absent fibers and lower-dimensional boundary
fibers, and never substitutes open caps for the closed cap H.

## 4. The half-capture threshold p<=1/2 suffices in every d>=2

Continue with the empty left strict residual, so(7) holds, and normalize
v_0=1. Let b=v_1. If the asserted midpoint inequality failed, then

    b>=f_1>2f_0=2(1-p)^(1/d)>=2^(1-1/d).                (8)

For every actually nonempty fiber C_-k, convexity and BM give

    v_-k <=1-k(b-1).                                    (9)

Indeed (C_-k+k C_1)/(k+1) is contained in C_0. This BM application uses
only nonempty sets; a boundary fiber of zero volume is allowed. A
negative right side means that fiber cannot be nonempty at all. Absent
fibers have no mass. Consequently the total left mass is at most
sum_(k>=1)[1-k(b-1)]_+^d. Independently, global maximality and ordinary
Grunbaum in the neighboring fiber give Q>=gamma b^d.

If d=2, then gamma=4/9 and(8) gives b>sqrt(2). Only k=1,2 can contribute
to the left mass, so

    Q <= p+sum_(j<0)|C_j|
       <=1/2+(2-sqrt(2))^2+(3-2sqrt(2))^2
       =47/2-16sqrt(2)<8/9<gamma b^2.

The strict numerical comparison is exact: it is equivalent to
sqrt(2)>407/288, and 407^2=165649<165888=2*288^2.

If d>=3, then(8) gives b>2^(1-1/d)>=2^(2/3)>3/2. Only k=1 can have
positive left mass, and that mass is less than (1/2)^d<=1/8. Thus

    Q<=1/2+1/8=5/8,
    Q>=gamma b^d>2^(d-1)/3>=4/3,

using gamma>1/3 from(4). This is also a contradiction. Therefore no
failure of(2) is possible under p<=1/2.

The inequality is in fact strict in this empty-neighbor case. For d=2,
the same mass comparison excludes b>=sqrt(2), while f_0>=1/sqrt(2).
For d>=3, b>=3/2 would already imply Q>=(1/3)(3/2)^d>=9/8, contrary
to Q<=5/8 (the possible second left fiber has volume zero at b=3/2).
Hence b<3/2 and f_0>=2^(-1/d)>3/4. In both cases f_0>b/2>=f_1/2.
Undoing the normalization and reflecting the integer coordinate gives
the assertion for either empty neighboring strict residual.

## 5. Quantitative reserve under the stronger p<=gamma hypothesis

For this section assume p<=gamma. Continue with the empty residual on
the left and normalize v_0=1;
all displayed masses are now divided by |C_0|. Let b=v_1>=0. We claim

    b<10/7.                                           (10)

There is nothing to prove if b=0. For any actually nonempty fiber at
base -k, k>=1, convexity gives

    (1/(k+1)) C_-k + (k/(k+1)) C_1 subset C_0.

Brunn--Minkowski, valid for these nonempty compact convex sets even
when C_-k has zero d-volume, implies

    v_-k <= (k+1)-k b = 1-k(b-1).                      (11)

If the right side is negative, that fiber cannot be nonempty. Absent
fibers contribute zero. Thus the total left mass is bounded by

    sum_(k>=1) |C_-k| <=sum_(k>=1) [1-k(b-1)]_+^d       (12)

whenever b>1.

Suppose b>=10/7. Only k=1,2 can have a positive right side, and

    sum_(k>=1)|C_-k|
       <=(4/7)^d+(1/7)^d<=17/49.                       (13)

On the other hand, the ordinary centroid of the full-dimensional
fiber C_1 has mixed raw depth at least gamma |C_1|: every ambient
halfspace containing that point captures at least the ordinary
Grunbaum fraction of its own fiber, with all other contributions
nonnegative. Pure integer halfspaces containing it include its whole
fiber. Global maximality of Q consequently gives Q>=gamma b^d.
Combining this with(7), p<=gamma, and(13) yields

    100 gamma/49 <= gamma b^d <= Q
                      <= gamma+17/49,

where b^d>=b^2>=100/49 because d>=2 and b>1. The resulting inequality
51 gamma<=17 contradicts gamma>1/3. This proves(10), without a noheavy
assumption or an assertion about the ordinary centroid of C.

Undo the normalization. The source residual root satisfies, by(1),(5),

    f_0=v_0(1-p)^(1/d)>=sqrt(5)v_0/3.

The left residual root is zero and f_1<=v_1<(10/7)v_0. Subtraction
proves precisely the reserve(3). The proof is symmetric if the right
neighboring strict residual is empty, including when both are empty.

## 6. Both neighboring strict residuals nonempty

It remains to justify(2) when both actual strict residual sets are
nonempty, including a possible lower-dimensional boundary fiber.
Choose nonempty compact convex subsets of those strict residuals:
one may intersect each fiber with the stricter inequality
u.x+a j<=b-epsilon for sufficiently small epsilon>0. If one set has
zero d-volume but is nonempty, it is still a valid BM summand.
Convexity and affinity give containment of their Minkowski midpoint
in the source strict residual. BM therefore bounds f_0 below by the
mean of their volume roots. As epsilon decreases to0, the compact
sets increase to the strict residuals; continuity from below of the
finite d-volume gives(2). This argument does not apply BM to an empty
set and does not discard boundary-only fibers as potential points in
a Minkowski sum.

The two alternatives, both neighboring strict residuals nonempty or
at least one empty, exhaust all cases and complete the proof. Section4
gives the main p<=1/2 result; Section5 gives the stated additional reserve.

## 7. Scope for the original residual program

The theorem is about the ACTUAL nearest-neighbor midpoint row at one
globally deepest source, for one actual critical cap satisfying the
own-fiber fraction condition p<=1/2 (which includes all caps with
p<=gamma).
It does not by itself control a terminal
row of a KKT absorbing chain: such a chain may visit other bases at
which the same cap is not critical, or its own captured fraction is
larger than1/2. Proving (2) at the source alone does not justify
optional stopping along those other states.

It explains why the exact d=1 affine-interval all-KKT counterexample
does not extend with its own fraction at most gamma_d to this local
critical comparison: d=1 violates the constants(4)--(5). Conversely,
it makes no claim that an arbitrary mixed-integer critical cap has a
small enough own-fiber captured fraction, so it does not eliminate
that hypothesis by an implicit centroid choice.
